claims.claim: Calibration within groups and balance of error rates cannot all hold when base rates differ, except in trivial cases.
claims.source: Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan (2016), Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores; Chouldechova (2017), Big Data 5(2).

concept_html:
A model can be accurate overall and fail one group. Before release, compute the key rates per subgroup: age band, region, sex, ethnicity where you hold it lawfully, and any group the decision affects differently.

Per group, report:

  • n and positives, so readers can judge the evidence.
  • Selection rate: the share flagged.
  • True positive rate (recall): the share of real positives flagged.
  • False positive rate: the share of real negatives flagged.
  • Precision, and a calibration check (lesson B12-L2).

Then face a hard fact. When groups have different base rates, a calibrated score cannot also give equal false positive and true positive rates, except in trivial cases (Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan, 2016; Chouldechova, 2017).

A simulation in this course's build: a perfectly calibrated score for two groups with base rates of 30% and 10%, one threshold of 0.3. In both groups, cases scored 0.3 to 0.4 were positive about 34% of the time. Yet group A had a true positive rate of 0.65 and a false positive rate of 0.39. Group B had 0.15 and 0.03.

So choose, with the people accountable for the decision, which property matters most for this use:

  • Equal calibration: a score means the same risk in every group.
  • Equal true positive rates: each group's genuine cases are found at the same rate. Suits allocating help.
  • Equal false positive rates: each group bears the same rate of wrong flags. Suits decisions with a cost to the flagged person.

Write the choice, the reasons and the measured gaps in the model card (lesson B18-L2).

Removing a protected attribute from the features does not remove its influence. Postcode, first name and shopping patterns act as proxies. Keep the attribute available for measuring, where lawful, even if the model never uses it.

lines: import pandas as pd
def group_rates(df: pd.DataFrame, group: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
"""Selection rate, TPR and FPR per group, with counts. Columns y and flagged are 0/1."""
rows = []
for name, g in df.groupby(group, sort=True):
pos, neg = g["y"] == 1, g["y"] == 0
flag = g["flagged"] == 1
rows.append({
group: name,
"n": len(g),
"positives": int(pos.sum()),
"selection_rate": float(flag.mean()),
"tpr": float((flag & pos).sum() / pos.sum()) if pos.sum() > 0 else None,
"fpr": float((flag & neg).sum() / neg.sum()) if neg.sum() > 0 else None,
})
return pd.DataFrame(rows)

import pandas as pd


def group_rates(df: pd.DataFrame, group: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Selection rate, TPR and FPR per group, with counts.

    Args:
        df: Columns y and flagged (0/1) and the group column.
        group: Name of the group column.

    Returns:
        One row per group, sorted by group.
    """
    rows = []
    for name, g in df.groupby(group, sort=True):
        pos, neg = g["y"] == 1, g["y"] == 0
        flag = g["flagged"] == 1
        rows.append(
            {
                group: name,
                "n": len(g),
                "positives": int(pos.sum()),
                "selection_rate": float(flag.mean()),
                "tpr": float((flag & pos).sum() / pos.sum()) if pos.sum() > 0 else None,
                "fpr": float((flag & neg).sum() / neg.sum()) if neg.sum() > 0 else None,
            }
        )
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

title: Performance by subgroup, and the fairness trade-offs
why_html: A hardship-support model flagged customers for proactive help. Overall recall was 0.62. By age band, customers over 70 had recall 0.28: they used fewer digital channels, so the features the model relied on were sparse for them. The group most likely to need help was the least likely to be offered it. A per-group table at validation showed the gap in one line.
